Ongoing protests caused authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at the main hub, Suvarnabhumi International Airport, which handles 60,000 incoming passengers daily, an assistant to airport director Serirat Prasutanond told CNN. Pro- and anti-government protesters also exchanged gunfire Tuesday, a Thai police official said. Protesters with golf clubs and long wooden sticks clashed with airport taxi drivers, with each side throwing objects at the other.  Watch what's causing the protests » . Protesters blockaded people trying to get to one of the airports. They directed travelers to exit onto the access roads.  See more photos » . "I'm trying to get out of this place, but I'm stuck," iReporter Arjan Sing, who was on a two-week vacation to India and stopped in Bangkok to visit a friend's family. "When we took the exit there were lots of tourists standing around wondering what they were going to do." Gannon said the situation started off fairly relaxed, but tensions were escalating. "As more and more tourists leave [the airport], the fact that we don't have any information and there's no one to give us information, now we feel stranded here and we don't know where to go," Gannon said. "It seems a little bit more hostile than it was earlier." Gannon said she's heard nothing from airport personnel and her quest for answers is hurt even more by the fact that many people in the airport speak no English. "I don't know what happened to my flight," one woman waiting in an airport told CNN. "They won't talk to us and I'm angry and sad because I have two small children and they're sick so we want to go home." The airlines have also been mum on the situation, Gannon said, making it difficult for them to decide whether to wait it out at the airport or try to find a hotel. "We've had absolutely no contact from our air carrier," Gannon said. "But that seems to be universal across the board." One traveler said the wait was frustrating. "They've started coming through and telling us that we possibly might be out of here in the morning," he told CNN. "But either way, there's no problem. We just sit here and relax and enjoy the ride." Gannon said she and her new spouse just hope to get home sometime in the near future. "We've been gone for 17 days and [the honeymoon] was good -- until now," she said. "We are just trying to go home, get back to work and Thanksgiving."

BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) -- After 17 hours, Kerri Gannon and her husband remained stranded in an airport in Bangkok, Thailand, on Wednesday, searching for a way home to the United States after the facility was overtaken by crowds of protesters and shut down.

Anti-government protesters gathered in front of Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi Airport early Wednesday. The newly married couple, who had traveled to Thailand for their honeymoon, struggled to find a way back to California after explosions at two Bangkok airports wounded four people and forced both facilities to close.

The previous day, thousands of anti-government protesters had stormed the airports to demonstrate against the return of Thai Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat from an economic summit in Peru.

"The upper level outside is really crowded with protesters, and for the most part they're kind of quiet and polite," Gannon reported from the airport. "They're roaming the airport, they're cheering and clapping and walking around, but it's clearly their domain."

It was unclear from which of the two occupied airports she was speaking, but tourists were stranded at both.

The People's Alliance for Democracy, which is leading the protests, has vowed not to end its occupation of the airports until the prime minister resigns. The group accuses his government of serving as a front for ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

The ongoing protests prompted authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at the main hub, Suvarnabhumi International Airport, which handles 60,000 arriving passengers daily, an assistant to airport director Serirat Prasutanond told CNN.

Pro- and anti-government demonstrators also exchanged gunfire on Tuesday, a Thai police official said. Protesters wielding golf clubs and long wooden sticks clashed with airport taxi drivers, with both sides hurling objects at one another.

Protesters blockaded people attempting to reach one of the airports, directing travelers to exit onto the access roads.

"I'm trying to get out of this place, but I'm stuck," said iReporter Arjan Sing, who was on a two-week vacation to India and had stopped in Bangkok to visit a friend's family. "When we took the exit, there were lots of tourists standing around wondering what they were going to do."

Gannon said the situation began fairly calmly, but tensions were escalating. "As more and more tourists leave [the airport], the fact that we don't have any information and there's no one to give us information -- now we feel stranded here and we don't know where to go," she said. "It seems a little bit more hostile than it was earlier."

Gannon noted that she had heard nothing from airport personnel, and her search for answers was further hindered by the fact that many people in the airport spoke no English.

"I don't know what happened to my flight," one woman waiting in the airport told CNN. "They won't talk to us, and I'm angry and sad because I have two small children and they're sick, so we want to go home."

The airlines, too, had remained silent about the situation, Gannon said, making it difficult for travelers to decide whether to wait it out at the airport or seek a hotel.

"We've had absolutely no contact from our air carrier," Gannon said. "But that seems to be universal across the board."

One traveler described the wait as frustrating. "They've started coming through and telling us that we possibly might be out of here in the morning," he told CNN. "But either way, there's no problem. We just sit here and relax and enjoy the ride."

Gannon said she and her new husband simply hoped to return home in the near future. "We've been gone for 17 days, and [the honeymoon] was good -- until now," she said. "We are just trying to go home, get back to work and Thanksgiving."

"Outside on the upper level it's packed with protesters, and mostly they're being fairly calm and courteous," Gannon reported from inside the airport. "They wander through the terminal, cheering and applauding as they move about, but there's no question they've taken control of the place."

She didn't specify which of the two seized airports she was calling from, though visitors were left stuck at both locations.

The organization behind the demonstrations, the People's Alliance for Democracy, declared that it would continue occupying the airports until Somchai stepped down. The group charges that his administration merely serves as a cover for Thaksin Shinawatra, the former prime minister who was removed from power.

Because of the persistent protests, officials called off every arriving and departing flight at Suvarnabhumi International Airport, the country's primary transportation hub, which processes 60,000 arriving travelers each day, according to an aide to airport director Serirat Prasutanond.

A Thai police official reported that gunfire was traded on Tuesday between demonstrators supporting the government and those against it. Protesters armed with golf clubs and lengthy wooden poles fought with airport taxi drivers, and both groups hurled items at one another.

Demonstrators blocked individuals attempting to reach one airport, steering travelers off toward the access roads instead.

"I'm trying to get away from here, but there's no way out," said iReporter Arjan Sing, who had been enjoying a two-week trip to India and had made a stopover in Bangkok to see the family of a friend. "When we headed for the exit, crowds of tourists were just standing there, unsure of what to do next."

According to Gannon, things began peacefully enough, but the mood was growing tenser. "With more and more tourists departing, and with nobody providing us any updates or information, we now feel completely stuck without any idea where to turn," she explained. "It appears somewhat more threatening now than it did earlier."

Gannon mentioned that no airport staff had communicated with her, and her efforts to get answers were further complicated because a large number of people at the airport didn't speak English at all.

"I have no idea what became of my flight," a woman waiting at the airport told CNN. "Nobody will speak with us, and I'm both furious and upset because I have two young children who are ill and we just want to return home."

Gannon said the airlines had likewise stayed silent about what was happening, leaving travelers unsure whether they should hold out at the terminal or search for a hotel room. "Our airline hasn't reached out to us at all," she noted. "But that appears to be the case for everyone here."

Another traveler described the delay as aggravating. "They've begun walking through and letting us know we might be able to leave by morning," he told CNN. "But it doesn't matter either way. We'll just sit tight, take it easy, and go with the flow."

Gannon said that she and her new husband simply wished to make it home sometime soon. "We've been away for 17 days now, and the honeymoon was wonderful -- right up until this," she said. "All we want is to head home, return to our jobs, and be there for Thanksgiving."

# American Tourists Stranded as Bangkok Airport Shutdown Enters Third Day

**BANGKOK, Thailand** — Thousands of travelers, including hundreds of Americans, remained stranded at Bangkok's two main airports Thursday as anti-government protesters continued their occupation, bringing air travel to a standstill in one of Southeast Asia's busiest transportation hubs.

The demonstrators, who oppose the current government, seized Suvarnabhumi International Airport earlier this week, forcing the cancellation of all commercial flights and leaving tourists scrambling for alternatives to get home.

## Honeymoon Turns to Nightmare

Among those caught in the chaos are Michael and Sarah Thompson, a newlywed couple from Denver, Colorado, who arrived in Thailand for what was supposed to be a dream honeymoon.

"We got married two weeks ago and thought this would be the trip of a lifetime," said Sarah Thompson, 28, sitting on the floor of a crowded hotel lobby near the airport. "Now we just want to get home. We've been trying to reach the U.S. Embassy, but the phone lines are overwhelmed."

Her husband Michael, 31, described their frustration navigating the uncertainty.

"Every time we hear a flight might be leaving, we rush to check, and then it falls through," he said. "We're running low on cash, our hotel is booked solid, and nobody can give us a straight answer about when the airport will reopen. It's scary being stuck somewhere with no clear way out."

## Embassy Response

The U.S. Embassy in Bangkok issued a statement urging American citizens to monitor local news and register with the State Department's travel alert system. Officials said they were working with Thai authorities and airlines to identify options for stranded citizens.

Some travelers have begun exploring overland routes to neighboring countries or alternative airports in cities such as Phuket and Chiang Mai, though transportation to these locations has been strained by surging demand.

## Economic Impact

The airport closures are expected to deal a significant blow to Thailand's vital tourism industry, which accounts for a substantial portion of the nation's economy. Industry analysts warn that the disruption could cost hundreds of millions of dollars and damage the country's reputation as a premier travel destination during the peak tourist season.

Airlines have advised passengers to contact them directly regarding rebooking and refunds, though many carriers have suspended operations indefinitely.

For the Thompsons and countless others, the wait continues.

"We just want to go home and start our lives together," Sarah said. "This isn't how we imagined it."

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Thousands Stranded as Anti-Government Protesters Seize Bangkok Airports

**BANGKOK, Thailand** — Thailand's political crisis deepened this week as anti-government demonstrators occupied Bangkok's two main airports, stranding an estimated 300,000 travelers and paralyzing one of Southeast Asia's most vital tourism and transport hubs.

## Airports Under Siege

Thousands of protesters from the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), identifiable by their signature yellow shirts, stormed Suvarnabhumi International Airport, forcing the suspension of all commercial flights. The nearby Don Mueang Airport, which had been handling domestic operations, was also overrun, effectively sealing off air access to the Thai capital.

Airport authorities announced the indefinite closure of Suvarnabhumi, a facility that normally handles more than 100,000 passengers daily. Departure halls that would ordinarily bustle with business travelers and tourists instead filled with demonstrators waving Thai flags and chanting slogans against the government.

## Travelers Caught in the Crossfire

For the hundreds of thousands of stranded passengers, the crisis has meant uncertainty, frustration, and mounting expense.

"We've been sleeping in hotel lobbies and waiting for any news," said one European tourist, echoing the sentiments of countless visitors caught in the standoff. "Nobody can tell us when we'll be able to fly home."

Foreign embassies scrambled to assist their nationals, while airlines diverted flights to alternative airports, including the resort island of Phuket and the U-Tapao naval airfield southeast of Bangkok. The Thai government worked to arrange emergency evacuation flights, but the sheer scale of the disruption overwhelmed contingency plans.

The economic damage rippled far beyond the airports. Thailand's crucial tourism industry, which accounts for roughly 6 percent of the nation's economy, faced devastating losses during what should have been peak high season.

## A Government Under Pressure

At the center of the storm stands Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat, whose government the PAD has vowed to topple. Protesters accuse Somchai of serving as a proxy for former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, the deeply divisive leader ousted in a 2006 military coup and later convicted of corruption. Somchai is Thaksin's brother-in-law, a connection his opponents cite as evidence of continued Thaksin influence over Thai politics.

The PAD, a loose coalition of royalists, businesspeople, and urban middle-class Thais, has demanded Somchai's resignation and called for fundamental changes to the country's electoral system, which they argue allows populist politicians to buy the votes of the rural poor.

Prime Minister Somchai, attending an economic summit in Peru at the time of the airport seizures, rejected calls to step down and declared a state of emergency at both airports. However, the declaration proved difficult to enforce, as security forces and police showed little willingness to forcibly remove the demonstrators.

## A Nation Divided

The airport occupation represents the dramatic culmination of months of escalating political confrontation that has exposed deep fault lines in Thai society — pitting the largely urban, establishment-aligned PAD against the rural support base that has repeatedly returned Thaksin-affiliated parties to power at the ballot box.

The standoff raised fears of wider violence, particularly as pro-government "red shirt" supporters mobilized in response. Observers watched anxiously for any sign of military intervention in a country with a long history of coups.

## Looking Ahead

As the crisis continued, all eyes turned to Thailand's Constitutional Court, which was weighing a case that could dissolve the ruling party over electoral fraud allegations — a ruling that could potentially force Somchai from office and offer a path out of the deadlock.

For the hundreds of thousands of travelers stranded far from home, however, resolution could not come soon enough.

*This is a developing story.*

# Stranded at Suvarnabhumi: Days of Confusion as Protesters Seize Bangkok's Airport

*A journalistic account of the 2008 airport occupation*

---

**BANGKOK** — When the yellow-shirted protesters first appeared in the departure halls of Suvarnabhumi International Airport on the evening of November 25, 2008, few of the thousands of travelers passing through understood they were witnessing the beginning of a siege that would strand an estimated 300,000 people and paralyze one of Southeast Asia's busiest aviation hubs.

What unfolded over the following days became a study in institutional breakdown—a cascade of silence, rumor, and mounting desperation that left travelers to navigate the crisis largely on their own.

## The First Hours

The occupation was carried out by the People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), a movement seeking to force the resignation of the government of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat. Demonstrators, many draped in the royal yellow that had become their signature, poured into the terminal and quickly overwhelmed a security presence that offered little resistance.

For passengers already checked in, the transformation was surreal.

"We were sitting at the gate waiting to board when people just started walking in—hundreds of them, with flags and whistles," recalled one Australian traveler who had been bound for Sydney. "There was no announcement, no security telling anyone what was happening. One minute it was a normal airport, the next it wasn't."

By that night, all outbound flights had ceased. The Airports of Thailand authority suspended operations, and Suvarnabhumi—a gleaming facility that had opened only two years earlier—fell under the control of the demonstrators.

## A Vacuum of Information

If a single thread united the accounts of those caught in the occupation, it was the near-total absence of reliable information.

Airline counters emptied of staff. Departure boards froze or displayed flights that would never leave. Announcements, when they came at all, were sporadic and often contradictory.

"Nobody could tell us anything," said a British couple who had been returning home after a holiday in Phuket. "Not the airline, not the airport, not our embassy at first. We were getting more information from text messages from family watching the news back home than from anyone standing ten feet away from us."

This informational void bred rumor. Travelers traded unverified reports: the airport would reopen in hours; the military was about to intervene; buses were coming; buses were not coming. Each rumor sent ripples of movement through the crowds, hope and disappointment cycling in waves.

For non-English speakers, the disorientation was compounded. Some travelers described relying on strangers to translate fragmentary news, forming impromptu communities of the stranded who pooled what little they knew.

## The Long Wait

As hours stretched into days, the practical realities of the siege pressed in. The terminal, designed for transit rather than habitation, strained under the weight of thousands with nowhere to go.

Food and water grew scarce and expensive. Travelers described sleeping on floors, on baggage carousels, on any available surface. Families with young children and elderly passengers faced particular hardship.

"You'd wake up—if you slept at all—stiff and dazed, and for a second forget where you were," one stranded traveler recounted. "Then you'd hear the whistles and the loudspeakers and remember. Another day."

Sanitation deteriorated. Charging a phone—the lifeline to the outside world and to loved ones—became a small daily struggle over limited outlets.

Money presented its own anxieties. Travelers who had budgeted for a departure found themselves burning through cash on overpriced meals and, for those who could find and afford them, hotel rooms far from the airport that required navigating a city they didn't know.

## Escalating Tension

The mood, several travelers noted, shifted as the days wore on. The initial bewilderment hardened into frustration, and frustration edged toward fear.

The protesters themselves, many travelers stressed, were not generally hostile toward foreigners; some described demonstrators handing out water or expressing apologies for the disruption. But the broader political situation was volatile and unpredictable, and the specter of violence hung over the scene.

"You could feel the tension changing," said one traveler who had been trying to reach Europe. "In the beginning people were annoyed. By day three, there was this undercurrent—what if this turns violent? What if the army comes in? Nobody knew, and that not-knowing was the worst part."

Reports of a bombing incident and clashes elsewhere in the standoff filtered through, amplifying anxieties. Travelers weighed impossible calculations: stay in the terminal and wait, or attempt the uncertain journey to alternative airports being hastily pressed into service.

## The Scramble to Leave

As the occupation dragged on with no clear resolution, governments and airlines began organizing evacuation efforts. Alternative airports, including the smaller U-Tapao airfield—a former military base—were mobilized to handle the desperate backlog.

But reaching them meant long, expensive road journeys through unfamiliar territory, often arranged through incomplete or conflicting instructions.

"Getting a flight out felt like winning a lottery you didn't understand the rules of," one traveler said. "You'd hear a plane was leaving from somewhere, you'd rush there, and then you'd wait again."

## Resolution

The siege ended after roughly a week, when a Constitutional Court ruling dissolved the ruling party and forced the prime minister from office—meeting a central demand of the protesters, who then announced they would leave the airport. Operations resumed gradually, and the enormous task of clearing the backlog of stranded passengers began.

For those who lived through it, the experience left a lasting impression—less of the political drama that had swirled around them than of the simple, grinding human experience of being stuck, uninformed, and uncertain.

"I've never felt so invisible," one traveler reflected. "All these people in charge, all these systems that are supposed to work, and none of it did. In the end you just had each other—strangers looking out for strangers, because that was all that was left."

---

*The 2008 occupation of Suvarnabhumi Airport stands as one of the most disruptive episodes in modern aviation history, a moment when a domestic political struggle stranded travelers from around the world and exposed how quickly the machinery of global transit can grind to a halt.*

**BANGKOK** — Explosions and violent clashes erupted at two of Bangkok's major airports today, throwing air travel into chaos and stranding thousands of international tourists as anti-government demonstrations escalated into their most dangerous phase yet.

Witnesses reported multiple blasts near the terminals, sending panicked travelers scrambling for cover as security forces struggled to contain surging crowds of protesters who had converged on the airports.

"We heard a loud bang and then people started running everywhere," said Emma Thornton, a British tourist who had been waiting to board a flight home. "Nobody knew what was happening. There was smoke, and children were crying. We just huddled in a corner not knowing if it was safe to move."

The disruptions have paralyzed operations at both airports, with airlines canceling or diverting flights and leaving passengers uncertain when—or how—they will be able to leave the country.

## Tourists Caught in the Crossfire

For many visitors, what began as a holiday has turned into a frightening ordeal.

"We've been sitting here for hours with no information," said Marco Bianchi, an Italian traveler stranded with his family. "The departure boards just say 'cancelled.' Staff are as confused as we are. We just want to get out safely."

Airport authorities set up temporary areas for stranded passengers, distributing water and blankets, but the sheer number of affected travelers overwhelmed available resources. Long lines formed at information desks, while others slept on floors surrounded by luggage.

Hotel operators near the airports reported being fully booked within hours as tourists sought refuge from the unrest.

## Background: Months of Political Turmoil

The airport violence marks a dramatic escalation in a political standoff that has gripped Thailand for months. Anti-government demonstrators, demanding sweeping changes to the country's leadership, have staged repeated mass protests, occupying government buildings and blocking key intersections in the capital.

The movement, which draws support from a broad coalition of political and civic groups, accuses the sitting government of corruption and illegitimacy. Government supporters, in turn, have mobilized their own counter-demonstrations, raising fears of wider civil conflict.

Tensions have simmered for weeks, punctuated by sporadic outbreaks of violence. Today's targeting of the airports—vital economic lifelines for a nation heavily dependent on tourism—represents a significant intensification of the crisis.

## Economic Fallout Looms

Analysts warn the airport shutdown could deal a severe blow to Thailand's tourism industry, one of the country's most important economic sectors.

"The images of chaos at the airports will be broadcast around the world," one travel industry observer noted. "The damage to Thailand's reputation as a safe destination could last well beyond the resolution of the current political crisis."

Foreign governments have begun issuing travel advisories, urging their citizens to exercise extreme caution and avoid the affected areas.

## What Happens Next

As night fell over Bangkok, the situation remained volatile. Security forces maintained a heavy presence around the airports, while protest leaders showed no signs of backing down.

Embassies scrambled to account for their nationals and explore options for evacuating stranded citizens.

"We just want to go home," Thornton said, her voice trembling. "This was supposed to be the trip of a lifetime."

# Protesters Storm Bangkok Airports Opposing PM's Return; Thousands Stranded

**BANGKOK** — Anti-government demonstrators surged into Bangkok's two main airports Tuesday, forcing the suspension of flights and stranding thousands of travelers, in an escalating protest against the prime minister's planned return to the country.

Waves of protesters, many wearing the movement's signature colors and waving national flags, breached security perimeters at Suvarnabhumi International Airport and the older Don Mueang Airport, chanting slogans and unfurling banners denouncing what they called an illegitimate attempt to reinstall the embattled leader.

Airport authorities halted departures as demonstrators occupied terminal concourses, while riot police maintained a tense standoff at entry points. No serious injuries were immediately reported, though scuffles broke out as some passengers tried to push through the crowds toward check-in counters.

## Chaos in the Terminals

Inside the main departure hall, the scene was one of confusion and mounting frustration. Families slept on floors surrounded by luggage, information boards flashed cancellation notices, and long lines snaked toward beleaguered airline service desks.

"We've been here since five o'clock this morning and no one can tell us anything," said Margaret Ellison, a retired teacher from Sacramento, California, who was traveling with her husband, Robert, at the end of a three-week vacation. "We just want to go home. We understand people have grievances with their government, but we're caught in the middle of something we don't understand."

Robert Ellison said the couple had spent their savings on the trip. "Our flight was supposed to leave at noon. Now they're saying maybe tomorrow, maybe the day after. The hotels near the airport are all full. We don't know where we're going to sleep tonight," he said, gesturing toward the crowded terminal floor.

Other stranded passengers echoed the sense of helplessness. A businessman from Singapore, who declined to give his name, said he had missed a critical meeting. "This is costing me thousands. I feel for the local people, but shutting down an international airport hurts ordinary travelers most," he said.

## Political Backdrop

The demonstrations mark the latest chapter in Thailand's long-running political turmoil, which has repeatedly pitted rival factions against one another and periodically spilled into the streets of the capital. Protesters say the prime minister's return would deepen a political crisis they argue undermines democratic institutions.

Movement leaders addressed the crowds through loudspeakers, vowing to maintain the occupation until their demands were met. "We will not stand aside and allow this," one organizer declared to cheers.

Government officials condemned the airport takeover, calling it an unlawful act that damaged the country's international reputation and economy. Tourism authorities warned that the disruption could deal a significant blow to an industry already navigating a difficult recovery.

## An Uncertain Wait

As night fell, the terminals remained crowded and flights suspended, with airlines advising passengers to stay away from the airports until further notice. Embassies, including the U.S. mission, issued advisories urging their citizens to monitor conditions and contact carriers directly.

For the Ellisons and countless others, the wait continued with no clear end in sight.

"We just keep watching the board and hoping," Margaret Ellison said. "All we can do is wait."
